transcript.content: Hello, please have a seat. What brings you in to see me today?

Thanks, doctor. What brings me in is... well, I just cannot keep my mind on one thing anymore. I'm a carpenter, you know, and it's getting dangerous, really. Just the other day, I was measuring out some baseboards—beautiful oak, actually, we got a great deal on it from a supplier down in Springfield. I love working with oak, the grain is just so... anyway, one saw starting up across the site, or somebody walking past the office window, or even just a thought popping into my head about another job we're bidding on, and boom. I'm pulled right off what I’m doing. Next thing I know, I'm looking for a pencil I left in the truck, and then I'm talking to the electrician about his dog, and the whole day just gets away from me. It's really frustrating. My husband says I've always been a little scatterbrained, but it's never been this bad. We went to this dog show last weekend, actually, speaking of dogs... but yeah, I just can't focus.
Have you noticed that you need much less sleep than usual while still feeling full of energy?

Less sleep? No, I wouldn't say that. I definitely don't feel full of extra energy, that's for sure. I sleep my regular amount. Though, speaking of sleeping, we actually just got this new mattress. It's one of those memory foam ones? Supposed to be great for your back, which I really need after hauling lumber all day. But anyway, to go with it, I started building us a new headboard out of reclaimed barn wood. I found this guy one town over who was tearing down an old silo, and the patina on this wood is just incredible. It's got these old square nails still stuck in some of the pieces. I spent like three hours on Tuesday just trying to pry one of them out without splitting the board, and my husband was like, why don't you just leave it in for character? Which, you know, makes sense, but... wait, what were you asking me about?

Physically restless? Well... I guess it depends on what I'm doing. If I'm out on a site, moving around, I'm okay. But if I have to sit at the desk doing estimates, or sit through a long meeting with the contractors, I feel... wound up inside. Like I just need to get up and move around. Which is funny, because I actually broke my wrist a couple years ago—fell off a ladder trying to reach a tricky corner on some crown molding. The doctor told me I had to take it easy, and I just couldn't stand it. Even now that it's healed, when I know I'm supposed to just stay put and finish the paperwork, I just feel this itch to get up. My husband tried to get me to do yoga to help with the sitting still, but the instructor had this really annoying voice, like she was talking to toddlers, you know? And the mats smelled weird. I just couldn't do it. But yeah, sitting still for long stretches just makes me feel like my motor's running and I'm stuck in park.

Interrupting people? Blurting things out? No, I wouldn't say I do that. If anything, I'm usually the quiet one just letting the other person talk. Or, well, I guess I'm standing there while they talk, but my mind is usually miles away. 

Like with this one client we have right now, Mrs. Gable. We're redoing her kitchen, and she will just talk your ear off. She ordered these custom brass drawer pulls all the way from Italy. Beautiful craftsmanship, honestly. They have this little intricate leaf pattern on the sides. But they weigh an absolute ton. I was telling my foreman we're going to have to reinforce all the drawer faces just to handle the weight of the hardware, otherwise in five years they'll be pulling the wood right apart. We usually use this specific wood glue for that kind of reinforcement, it sets in like twenty minutes, but you have to make sure you clamp it perfectly straight because once it cures, you are not getting it apart without a chisel. I actually broke my favorite chisel last month trying to fix a mistake one of the new guys made on a door frame... 

Wait, I'm sorry. What did you ask me? Did you ask about talking to clients?
Do you find yourself constantly worrying about many different everyday things, and having trouble controlling that worry?

Worrying? No, not really. I'm not much of a worrier about everyday stuff. I just kind of take things as they come. My husband is the one who worries about all the little things, like the bills and the groceries. 

Speaking of groceries, we went to this outdoor market on Sunday and I saw a guy there selling these hand-turned wooden bowls. Really beautiful shape to them, made out of black walnut, I'm pretty sure. But he finished them with this thick, high-gloss polyurethane, which is just... well, it's a crime for walnut. You really want to use a natural oil finish, like pure tung oil, to just let the natural grain speak for itself. I actually have a whole gallon of it sitting in my shop right now for a custom dining table I'm building. It's a massive piece, going to seat twelve. We actually had to go in and sister the floor joists in the client's dining room just so the floor wouldn't sag under the weight of it over the years. Working in a crawlspace with only two feet of clearance is absolutely brutal on the knees, let me tell you... 

Wait. I'm sorry, what were we talking about? Did you ask about my husband?

Waiting my turn? Like in lines or something? No, I don't think so. I mean, nobody likes waiting, right? But I just pull out my phone or look around. I'm pretty patient. 

Actually, speaking of waiting, I was at the lumber yard yesterday waiting for them to bring around this order of white oak. I had requested quarter-sawn because it has those beautiful medullary rays—those little flecks that catch the light, you know? It's so much more stable than plain-sawn, especially for cabinet doors. If you use plain-sawn for a wide panel, it's just going to cup on you the second the humidity changes. Anyway, while I was waiting, I saw this guy trying to load a stack of drywall into the back of a short-bed pickup without strapping it down right. He just tossed a single bungee cord over it. I had to go over and show him how to throw a proper trucker's hitch. You learn that knot once and you use it for the rest of your life. My dad taught it to me when I was maybe ten, tying down a canoe on top of his old station wagon...
